studies.title: Developmental influences on the neural bases of responses to social rejection: implications of social neuroscience for education.
studies.abstract: Relational aggression such as social rejection is common within school peer groups. Converging evidence suggests that adolescent females are particularly sensitive to social rejection. We used a novel fMRI adaptation of the Cyberball social rejection paradigm to investigate the neural response to social rejection in 19 mid-adolescent (aged 14-16) and 16 adult female participants. Across all participants, social exclusion (relative to inclusion) elicited a response in bilateral medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC) extending into ventral and subgenual anterior cingulate cortex and medial orbitofrontal cortex; and the left ventrolateral PFC (vlPFC); regions that have been associated in previous studies with social evaluation, negative affective processing, and affect regulation respectively. However, the exclusion-related response in right vlPFC, a region associated in previous studies with the regulation of rejection-related distress, was attenuated in adolescents. Within mPFC, greater activation during exclusion vs. inclusion was associated with greater self-reported susceptibility to peer influence in adolescents but not in adults. This suggests that the brain's response to experimentally-induced social rejection relates to adolescent behaviour in real-world social interactions. We speculate about the potential implications of these findings for educational settings. In particular, functional development of affective circuitry during adolescence may influence social interaction within the school peer group.

studies.title: Similar brain networks for detecting visuo-motor and visuo-proprioceptive synchrony.
studies.abstract: The ability to recognize feedback from own movement as opposed to the movement of someone else is important for motor control and social interaction. The neural processes involved in feedback recognition are incompletely understood. Two competing hypotheses have been proposed: the stimulus is compared with either (a) the proprioceptive feedback or with (b) the motor command and if they match, then the external stimulus is identified as feedback. Hypothesis (a) predicts that the neural mechanisms or brain areas involved in distinguishing self from other during passive and active movement are similar, whereas hypothesis (b) predicts that they are different. In this fMRI study, healthy subjects saw visual cursor movement that was either synchronous or asynchronous with their active or passive finger movements. The aim was to identify the brain areas where the neural activity depended on whether the visual stimulus was feedback from own movement and to contrast the functional activation maps for active and passive movement. We found activity increases in the right temporoparietal cortex in the condition with asynchronous relative to synchronous visual feedback from both active and passive movements. However, no statistically significant difference was found between these sets of activated areas when the active and passive movement conditions were compared. With a posterior probability of 0.95, no brain voxel had a contrast effect above 0.11% of the whole-brain mean signal. These results do not support the hypothesis that recognition of visual feedback during active and passive movement relies on different brain areas.

studies.title: Autism spectrum traits predict the neural response to eye gaze in typical individuals.
studies.abstract: Autism Spectrum Disorders (ASD) are neurodevelopmental disorders characterised by impaired social interaction and communication, restricted interests and repetitive behaviours. The severity of these characteristics are posited to lie on a continuum extending into the typical population, and typical adults' performance on behavioural tasks that are impaired in ASD is correlated with the extent to which they display autistic traits (as measured by Autism Spectrum Quotient, AQ). Individuals with ASD also show structural and functional differences in brain regions involved in social perception. Here we show that variation in AQ in typically developing individuals is associated with altered brain activity in the neural circuit for social attention perception while viewing others' eye gaze. In an fMRI experiment, participants viewed faces looking at variable or constant directions. In control conditions, only the eye region was presented or the heads were shown with eyes closed but oriented at variable or constant directions. The response to faces with variable vs. constant eye gaze direction was associated with AQ scores in a number of regions (posterior superior temporal sulcus, intraparietal sulcus, temporoparietal junction, amygdala, and MT/V5) of the brain network for social attention perception. No such effect was observed for heads with eyes closed or when only the eyes were presented. The results demonstrate a relationship between neurophysiology and autism spectrum traits in the typical (non-ASD) population and suggest that changes in the functioning of the neural circuit for social attention perception is associated with an extended autism spectrum in the typical population.

studies.title: Brain activity correlates with emotional perception induced by dynamic avatars.
studies.abstract: An accurate judgment of the emotional state of others is a prerequisite for successful social interaction and hence survival. Thus, it is not surprising that we are highly skilled at recognizing the emotions of others. Here we aimed to examine the neuronal correlates of emotion recognition from gait. To this end we created highly controlled dynamic body-movement stimuli based on real human motion-capture data (Roether et al., 2009). These animated avatars displayed gait in four emotional (happy, angry, fearful, and sad) and speed-matched neutral styles. For each emotional gait and its equivalent neutral gait, avatars were displayed at five morphing levels between the two. Subjects underwent fMRI scanning while classifying the emotions and the emotional intensity levels expressed by the avatars. Our results revealed robust brain selectivity to emotional compared to neutral gait stimuli in brain regions which are involved in emotion and biological motion processing, such as the extrastriate body area (EBA), fusiform body area (FBA), superior temporal sulcus (STS), and the amygdala (AMG). Brain activity in the amygdala reflected emotional awareness: for visually identical stimuli it showed amplified stronger response when the stimulus was perceived as emotional. Notably, in avatars gradually morphed along an emotional expression axis there was a parametric correlation between amygdala activity and emotional intensity. This study extends the mapping of emotional decoding in the human brain to the domain of highly controlled dynamic biological motion. Our results highlight an extensive level of brain processing of emotional information related to body language, which relies mostly on body kinematics.

studies.title: A frontotemporoparietal network common to initiating and responding to joint attention bids.
studies.abstract: Joint attention is a fundamental cognitive ability that supports daily interpersonal relationships and communication. The Parallel Distributed Processing model (PDPM) postulates that responding to (RJA) and initiating (IJA) joint attention are predominantly supported by posterior-parietal and frontal regions respectively. It also argues that these neural networks integrate during development, supporting the parallel processes of self- and other-attention representation during interactions. However, direct evidence for the PDPM is limited due to a lack of ecologically valid experimental paradigms that can capture both RJA and IJA. Building on existing interactive approaches, we developed a virtual reality paradigm where participants engaged in an online interaction to complete a cooperative task. By including tightly controlled baseline conditions to remove activity associated with non-social task demands, we were able to directly contrast the neural correlates of RJA and IJA to determine whether these processes are supported by common brain regions. Both RJA and IJA activated broad frontotemporoparietal networks. Critically, a conjunction analysis identified that a subset of these regions were common to both RJA and IJA. This right-lateralised network included the dorsal portion of the middle frontal gyrus (MFG), inferior frontal gyrus (IFG), middle temporal gyrus (MTG), precentral gyrus, posterior superior temporal sulcus (pSTS), temporoparietal junction (TPJ) and precuneus. Additional activation was observed in this network for IJA relative to RJA at MFG, IFG, TPJ and precuneus. This is the first imaging study to directly investigate the neural correlates common to RJA and IJA engagement, and thus support the assumption that a broad integrated network underlies the parallel aspects of both initiating and responding to joint attention.

studies.title: Right supramarginal gyrus is crucial to overcome emotional egocentricity bias in social judgments.
studies.abstract: Humans tend to use the self as a reference point to perceive the world and gain information about other people's mental states. However, applying such a self-referential projection mechanism in situations where it is inappropriate can result in egocentrically biased judgments. To assess egocentricity bias in the emotional domain (EEB), we developed a novel visuo-tactile paradigm assessing the degree to which empathic judgments are biased by one's own emotions if they are incongruent to those of the person we empathize with. A first behavioral experiment confirmed the existence of such EEB, and two independent fMRI experiments revealed that overcoming biased empathic judgments is associated with increased activation in the right supramarginal gyrus (rSMG), in a location distinct from activations in right temporoparietal junction reported in previous social cognition studies. Using temporary disruption of rSMG with repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation resulted in a substantial increase of EEB, and so did reducing visuo-tactile stimulation time as shown in an additional behavioral experiment. Our findings provide converging evidence from multiple methods and experiments that rSMG is crucial for overcoming emotional egocentricity. Effective connectivity analyses suggest that this may be achieved by early perceptual regulation processes disambiguating proprioceptive first-person information (touch) from exteroceptive third-person information (vision) during incongruency between self- and other-related affective states. Our study extends previous models of social cognition. It shows that although shared neural networks may underlie emotional understanding in some situations, an additional mechanism subserved by rSMG is needed to avoid biased social judgments in other situations.

studies.title: fMRI evidence of neural abnormalities in the subcortical face processing system in ASD.
studies.abstract: Recent evidence suggests that a rapid, automatic face detection system is supported by subcortical structures including the amygdala, pulvinar, and superior colliculus. Early-emerging abnormalities in these structures may be related to reduced social orienting in children with autism, and subsequently, to aberrant development of cortical circuits involved in face processing. Our objective was to determine whether functional abnormalities in the subcortical face processing system are present in adults with autism spectrum disorders (ASD) during supraliminal fearful face processing. Participants included twenty-eight individuals with ASD and 25 controls group-matched on age, IQ, and behavioral performance. The ASD group met diagnostic criteria on the ADI-R, ADOS-G, and DSM-IV. Both the ASD and control groups showed significant activation in bilateral fusiform gyri. The control group exhibited additional significant responses in the right amygdala, right pulvinar, and bilateral superior colliculi. In the direct group comparison, the controls showed significantly greater activation in the left amygdala, bilateral fusiform gyrus, right pulvinar, and bilateral superior colliculi. No brain region showed significantly greater activation in the ASD group compared to the controls. Thus, basic rapid face identification mechanisms appear to be functional in ASD. However, individuals with ASD failed to engage the subcortical brain regions involved in face detection and automatic emotional face processing, suggesting a core mechanism for impaired socioemotional processing in ASD. Neural abnormalities in this system may contribute to early-emerging deficits in social orienting and attention, the putative precursors to abnormalities in social cognition and cortical face processing specialization.

studies.title: Do implicit and explicit belief processing share neural substrates?
studies.abstract: Humans rely on their ability to infer another person's mental state to understand and predict others' behavior ("theory of mind," ToM). Multiple lines of research suggest that not only are humans able to consciously process another person's belief state, but also are able to do so implicitly. Here we explored how general implicit belief states are represented in the brain, compared to those substrates involved in explicit ToM processes. Previous work on this topic has yielded conflicting results, and thus, the extent to which the implicit and explicit ToM systems draw on common neural bases is unclear. Participants were presented with "Sally-Anne" type movies in which a protagonist was falsely led to believe a ball was in one location, only for a puppet to later move it to another location in their absence (false-belief condition). In other movies, the protagonist had their back turned the entire time the puppet moved the ball between the two locations, meaning that they had no opportunity to develop any pre-existing beliefs about the scenario (no-belief condition). Using a group of independently localized explicit ToM brain regions, we found greater activity for false-belief trials, relative to no-belief trials, in the right temporoparietal junction, right superior temporal sulcus, precuneus, and left middle prefrontal gyrus. These findings extend upon previous work on the neural bases of implicit ToM by showing substantial overlap between this system and the explicit ToM system, suggesting that both abilities might recruit a common set of mentalizing processes/functional brain regions. studies.title: Social gating of sensory information during ongoing communication.
studies.abstract: Social context plays an important role in human communication. Depending on the nature of the source, the same communication signal might be processed in fundamentally different ways. However, the selective modulation (or "gating") of the flow of neural information during communication is not fully understood. Here, we use multivoxel pattern analysis (MVPA) and multivoxel connectivity analysis (MVCA), a novel technique that allows to analyse context-dependent changes of the strength interregional coupling between ensembles of voxels, to examine how the human brain differentially gates content-specific sensory information during ongoing perception of communication signals. In a simulated electronic communication experiment, participants received two alternative text messages during fMRI ("happy" or "sad") which they believed had been sent either by their real-life friend outside the scanner or by a computer. A region in the dorsal medial prefrontal cortex (dmPFC) selectively increased its functional coupling with sensory-content encoding regions in the visual cortex when a text message was perceived as being sent by the participant's friend, and decreased its functional coupling with these regions when a text message was perceived as being sent by the computer. Furthermore, the strength of neural encoding of content-specific information of text messages in the dmPFC was modulated by the social tie between the participant and her friend: the more of her spare time a participant reported to spend with her friend the stronger was the neural encoding. This suggests that the human brain selectively gates sensory information into the relevant network for processing the mental states of others, depending on the source of the communication signal.

studies.title: Shifted inferior frontal laterality in women with major depressive disorder is related to emotion-processing deficits.
studies.abstract: Facial emotion perception (FEP) is a critical human skill for successful social interaction, and a substantial body of literature suggests that explicit FEP is disrupted in major depressive disorder (MDD). Prior research suggests that weakness in FEP may be an important phenomenon underlying patterns of emotion-processing challenges in MDD and the disproportionate frequency of MDD in women. Method Women with (n = 24) and without (n = 22) MDD, equivalent in age and education, completed a FEP task during functional magnetic resonance imaging.
studies.abstract_screening_reason: Abstract reports an fMRI study of facial emotion perception (a social-related task) and includes a group without MDD (healthy controls). studies.title: Functional parcellation of the human primary somatosensory cortex to natural touch.
studies.abstract: Despite the significance of human touch, brain responses to interpersonal manual touch have been rarely investigated. We used functional magnetic resonance imaging to study brain activity in eight healthy adults whose left hand was touched by two individuals, in separate runs and in 20-s blocks, either by holding, smoothing, or poking. Acceleration was measured from both the subject's and the touching person's hands for postimaging control of the stimuli. Independent component analysis of the functional magnetic resonance imaging data unraveled three functional networks involving the primary somatosensory cortex (SI). One network comprised the contralateral and another the ipsilateral Brodmann area 3. The third network included area 2 bilaterally, left-hemisphere middle temporal gyrus and dorsolateral prefrontal regions, ventral prefrontal cortices bilaterally, and middle cingulate cortex. The response shapes and polarities varied between the three networks. The contralateral area 3 differentiated the responses between the three types of touch stimuli, and the response magnitudes depended on the variability of the touch within each block. However, the responses of the other two networks were strikingly similar to all stimuli. The subjects' reports on the pleasantness of the touch did not correlate with the characteristics of the SI responses. These findings imply area-specific processing of the natural human touch in three networks including the SI cortex, with only area 2 connected to a functional network of brain areas that may support social interaction.
studies.abstract_screening_reason: This fMRI study measured brain responses while healthy adult participants received interpersonal manual touch from other people—an inherently social stimulus involving perception/processing of others. It clearly uses fMRI during a social-related task and includes healthy adults, satisfying both inclusion criteria.
studies.fulltext_screening_reason: This task-based fMRI study investigates processing of natural interpersonal touch (touch delivered by another person), which is a social-related stimulus (social communication/affiliation). Although analyses used ICA rather than a standard GLM contrast, the reported group spatial maps and stimulus-related effects satisfy the requirement for whole-brain task activation evidence. The paper is empirical, not ROI-only, and reports healthy-group results explicitly. Therefore it meets inclusion criteria I3, I4, I5, and I6.

studies.title: Oxytocin influences processing of socially relevant cues in the ventral tegmental area of the human brain.
studies.abstract: Evidence accumulates that the neuropeptide oxytocin plays an important role in mediating social interaction among humans and that a dysfunction in oxytocin-modulated brain mechanisms might lie at the core of disturbed social behavior in neuropsychiatric disease. Explanatory models suggest that oxytocin guides social approach and avoidance by modulating the perceived salience of socially meaningful cues. Animal data point toward the ventral tegmental area (VTA) as the brain site where this modulation takes place.

studies.title: Differences in Neural Response to Romantic Stimuli in Monogamous and Non-Monogamous Men.
studies.abstract: In non-human animal research, studies comparing socially monogamous and promiscuous species of voles (Microtus) have identified some key neural differences related to monogamy and non-monogamy. Specifically, densities of the vasopressin V1a receptor and dopamine D2 receptors in subcortical reward-related and limbic areas of the brain have been linked to monogamous behavior in prairie voles (Microtus ochrogaster). Similar brain areas have been shown to be correlated with feelings of romantic love in monogamously pair-bonded humans. Humans vary in the degree to which they engage in (non-)monogamous behaviors. The present study examined the differences in neural activation in response to sexual and romantic stimuli in monogamous (n = 10) and non-monogamous (n = 10) men. Results indicated that monogamous men showed more reward-related neural activity when viewing romantic pictures compared to non-monogamous men. Areas with increased activation for monogamous men were all in the right hemisphere and included the thalamus, accumbens, striatum, pallidum, insula, and orbitofrontal cortex. There were no significant differences between groups in activation to sexual stimuli. These results demonstrate that the neural processing of romantic images is different for monogamous and non-monogamous men. There is some overlap in the neural areas showing increased activation in monogamous men in the present study and the neural areas that show differences in the vole models of monogamy and affiliation. Future research will be needed to clarify whether similar factors are contributing to the neural differences seen in monogamous and non-monogamous humans and voles.

studies.title: Sex differences in the neural and behavioral response to intranasal oxytocin and vasopressin during human social interaction.
studies.abstract: Both oxytocin (OT) and vasopressin (AVP) are known to modulate social behavior, and dysfunction in both systems has been postulated as a potential cause of certain psychiatric disorders that involve social behavioral deficits. In particular, there is growing interest in intranasal OT as a potential treatment for certain psychiatric disorders, and preliminary pre-clinical and clinical studies suggest efficacy in alleviating some of the associated symptoms. However, the vast majority of research participants in these studies have been male, and there is evidence for sexually differentiated effects of nonapeptides in both humans and non-human animals. To date, no study has investigated the effect of intranasal OT on brain function in human males and females within the same paradigm. Previously, in a randomized, placebo-controlled, double-blind fMRI study, we reported effects of intranasal OT and AVP on behavior and brain activity of human males as they played an interactive social game known as the Prisoner's Dilemma Game. Here, we present findings from an identical study in human females, and compare these with our findings from males. Overall, we find that both behavioral and neural responses to intranasal OT and AVP are highly sexually differentiated. In women, AVP increased conciliatory behavior, and both OT and AVP caused women to treat computer partners more like humans. In men, AVP increased reciprocation of cooperation from both human and computer partners. However, no specific drug effects on behavior were shared between men and women. During cooperative interactions, both OT and AVP increased brain activity in men within areas rich in OT and AVP receptors and in areas playing a key role in reward, social bonding, arousal and memory (e.g., the striatum, basal forebrain, insula, amygdala and hippocampus), whereas OT and AVP either had no effect or in some cases actually decreased brain activity in these regions in women. OT treatment rendered neural responses of males more similar to responses of females in the placebo group and vice versa, raising the prospect of an inverted u-shaped dose response to central OT levels. These findings emphasize the need to fully characterize the effects of intranasal OT and AVP in both males and females and at multiple doses before widespread clinical application will be warranted.
studies.abstract_screening_reason: Randomized, placebo-controlled fMRI study using the Prisoner’s Dilemma (a social interaction task) in human male and female adults, meeting I1 and I2. Not a review (E1 not met). Abstract provides sufficient information to include for full-text review.

studies.title: Amygdala dysfunction in men with the fragile X premutation.
studies.abstract: Premutation alleles (55-200 CGG repeats) of the fragile X mental retardation 1 (FMR1) gene are associated with autism spectrum disorder in childhood, premature ovarian failure, and the neurodegenerative disorder, fragile X-associated tremor/ataxia syndrome (FXTAS). FXTAS, and perhaps the other clinical presentations among carriers, are thought to be due to toxic gain-of-function of elevated levels of the expanded-repeat FMR1 mRNA. Previous structural MRI studies have implicated the amygdala as a potential site of dysfunction underlying social deficits and/or risk for FXTAS. As a preliminary investigation of this possible association, adult males with the premutation, and male controls matched for IQ, age and education, completed three protocols that probe amygdala and sympathetic function: (i) a functional MRI paradigm that measures brain response to fearful faces; (ii) a fear-potentiated startle paradigm that differentiates responses to fearful faces and fearful non-social images and (iii) measurement of skin conductance level during a brief social encounter. Compared with controls, men with the FMR1 premutation demonstrated diminished brain activation in the amygdala and several brain areas that mediate social cognition while viewing fearful faces. The reduced amygdala activation in the premutation group was significantly associated with self-report of psychological symptoms on the Symptom Checklist-90--Revised. These men also displayed a lack of startle potentiation while viewing fearful faces and showed reduced skin conductance response when greeting an unfamiliar experimenter in comparison with the control group. The current findings may be related to social cognition deficits reported previously in children and adults with the premutation. The aetiology for this dysfunction may be elevated FMR1 mRNA or reduced FMR1 protein that occurs in carriers with higher premutation CGG repeat alleles.
studies.abstract_screening_reason: Abstract reports an fMRI paradigm measuring brain response to fearful faces (social-related task) and includes a healthy adult male control group matched for age/IQ/education. studies.title: Criticism hurts everybody, praise only some: Common and specific neural responses to approving and disapproving social-evaluative videos.
studies.abstract: Social evaluation is a ubiquitous feature of daily interpersonal interactions and can produce strong positive or negative emotional reactions. While previous research has highlighted neural correlates of static or dynamic facial expressions, little is known about neural processing of more naturalistic social interaction simulations or the modulating role of inter-individual differences such as trait fear of negative/positive evaluation. The present fMRI study investigated neural activity of 37 (21 female) healthy participants while watching videos of posers expressing a range of positive, negative, and neutral statements tapping into several basic and social emotions. Unpleasantness ratings linearly increased in response to positive to neutral to negative videos whereas arousal ratings were elevated in both emotional video conditions. At the whole brain level, medial prefrontal and rostral anterior cingulate cortex activated strongly in both emotional conditions which may be attributed to the cognitive processing demands of responding to complex social evaluation. Region of interest analysis for basic emotion processing areas revealed enhanced amygdala activation in both emotional conditions, whereas anterior and posterior insula showed stronger activity during negative evaluations only. Individuals with high fear of positive evaluation were characterized by increased posterior insula activity during positive videos, suggesting heightened interoception. Taken together, these results replicate and extend studies that used facial expression stimuli and reveal neurobiological systems involved in processing of more complex social-evaluative videos. Results also point to vulnerability factors for social-interaction related psychopathologies.
studies.abstract_screening_reason: fMRI study of social evaluation using videos in a sample of 37 healthy participants; directly investigates neural processing of social-related stimuli (social evaluation), meeting the review objective. studies.title: Seeing it my way or your way: frontoparietal brain areas sustain viewpoint-independent perspective selection processes.
studies.abstract: A hallmark of human social interaction is the ability to consider other people's mental states, such as what they see, believe, or desire. Prior neuroimaging research has predominantly investigated the neural mechanisms involved in computing one's own or another person's perspective and largely ignored the question of perspective selection. That is, which brain regions are engaged in the process of selecting between self and other perspectives? To address this question, the current fMRI study used a behavioral paradigm that required participants to select between competing visual perspectives. We provide two main extensions to current knowledge. First, we demonstrate that brain regions within dorsolateral prefrontal and parietal cortices respond in a viewpoint-independent manner during the selection of task-relevant over task-irrelevant perspectives. More specifically, following the computation of two competing visual perspectives, common regions of frontoparietal cortex are engaged to select one's own viewpoint over another's as well as select another's viewpoint over one's own. Second, in the absence of conflict between the content of competing perspectives, we showed a reduced engagement of frontoparietal cortex when judging another's visual perspective relative to one's own. This latter finding provides the first brain-based evidence for the hypothesis that, in some situations, another person's perspective is automatically and effortlessly computed, and thus, less cognitive control is required to select it over one's own perspective. In doing so, we provide stronger evidence for the claim that we not only automatically compute what other people see but also, in some cases, we compute this even before we are explicitly aware of our own perspective.

studies.title: Theory of mind broad and narrow: reasoning about social exchange engages ToM areas, precautionary reasoning does not.
studies.abstract: Baron-Cohen (1995) proposed that the theory of mind (ToM) inference system evolved to promote strategic social interaction. Social exchange--a form of co-operation for mutual benefit--involves strategic social interaction and requires ToM inferences about the contents of other individuals' mental states, especially their desires, goals, and intentions. There are behavioral and neuropsychological dissociations between reasoning about social exchange and reasoning about equivalent problems tapping other, more general content domains. It has therefore been proposed that social exchange behavior is regulated by social contract algorithms: a domain-specific inference system that is functionally specialized for reasoning about social exchange. We report an fMRI study using the Wason selection task that provides further support for this hypothesis. Precautionary rules share so many properties with social exchange rules--they are conditional, deontic, and involve subjective utilities--that most reasoning theories claim they are processed by the same neurocomputational machinery. Nevertheless, neuroimaging shows that reasoning about social exchange activates brain areas not activated by reasoning about precautionary rules, and vice versa. As predicted, neural correlates of ToM (anterior and posterior temporal cortex) were activated when subjects interpreted social exchange rules, but not precautionary rules (where ToM inferences are unnecessary). We argue that the interaction between ToM and social contract algorithms can be reciprocal: social contract algorithms requires ToM inferences, but their functional logic also allows ToM inferences to be made. By considering interactions between ToM in the narrower sense (belief-desire reasoning) and all the social inference systems that create the logic of human social interaction--ones that enable as well as use inferences about the content of mental states--a broader conception of ToM may emerge: a computational model embodying a Theory of Human Nature (ToHN).

studies.title: Regional brain responses in nulliparous women to emotional infant stimuli.
studies.abstract: Infant cries and facial expressions influence social interactions and elicit caretaking behaviors from adults. Recent neuroimaging studies suggest that neural responses to infant stimuli involve brain regions that process rewards. However, these studies have yet to investigate individual differences in tendencies to engage or withdraw from motivationally relevant stimuli. To investigate this, we used event-related fMRI to scan 17 nulliparous women. Participants were presented with novel infant cries of two distress levels (low and high) and unknown infant faces of varying affect (happy, sad, and neutral) in a randomized, counter-balanced order. Brain activation was subsequently correlated with scores on the Behavioral Inhibition System/Behavioral Activation System scale. Infant cries activated bilateral superior and middle temporal gyri (STG and MTG) and precentral and postcentral gyri. Activation was greater in bilateral temporal cortices for low- relative to high-distress cries. Happy relative to neutral faces activated the ventral striatum, caudate, ventromedial prefrontal, and orbitofrontal cortices. Sad versus neutral faces activated the precuneus, cuneus, and posterior cingulate cortex, and behavioral activation drive correlated with occipital cortical activations in this contrast. Behavioral inhibition correlated with activation in the right STG for high- and low-distress cries relative to pink noise. Behavioral drive correlated inversely with putamen, caudate, and thalamic activations for the comparison of high-distress cries to pink noise. Reward-responsiveness correlated with activation in the left precentral gyrus during the perception of low-distress cries relative to pink noise. Our findings indicate that infant cry stimuli elicit activations in areas implicated in auditory processing and social cognition. Happy infant faces may be encoded as rewarding, whereas sad faces activate regions associated with empathic processing. studies.title: Effects of a genome-wide supported psychosis risk variant on neural activation during a theory-of-mind task.
studies.abstract: Schizophrenia is associated with marked deficits in theory of mind (ToM), a higher-order form of social cognition representing the thoughts, emotions and intentions of others. Altered brain activation in the medial prefrontal cortex and temporo-parietal cortex during ToM tasks has been found in patients with schizophrenia, but the relevance of these neuroimaging findings for the heritable risk for schizophrenia is unclear. We tested the hypothesis that activation of the ToM network is altered in healthy risk allele carriers of the single-nucleotide polymorphism rs1344706 in the gene ZNF804A, a recently discovered risk variant for psychosis with genome-wide support. In all, 109 healthy volunteers of both sexes in Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium for rs1344706 were investigated with functional magnetic resonance imaging during a ToM task. As hypothesised, risk carriers exhibited a significant (P<0.05 false discovery rate, corrected for multiple comparisons) risk allele dose effect on neural activity in the medial prefrontal cortex and left temporo-parietal cortex. Moreover, the same effect was found in the left inferior parietal cortex and left inferior frontal cortex, which are part of the human analogue of the mirror neuron system. In addition, in an exploratory analysis (P<0.001 uncorrected), we found evidence for aberrant functional connectivity between the frontal and temporo-parietal regions in risk allele carriers. To conclude, we show that a dysfunction of the ToM network is associated with a genome-wide supported genetic risk variant for schizophrenia and has promise as an intermediate phenotype that can be mined for the development of biological interventions targeted to social dysfunction in psychiatry.

studies.title: Differential role of the Mentalizing and the Mirror Neuron system in the imitation of communicative gestures.
studies.abstract: Successful social interaction requires recognising the intention of another person's communicative gestures. At a neural level, this process may involve neural activity in different systems, such as the mentalizing system (MS) and the mirror neuron system (MNS). The aim of the present study was to explore the neural correlates of communicative gestures during observation and execution of these gestures. Twenty participants watched video clips of an actor executing social gestures (S), non-social gestures (NS) and meaningless gestures (ML). During fMRI data acquisition, participants were asked to observe (O) and subsequently to execute (E) one of two tasks: imitate the gesture presented (IMI) or perform a motor control task (CT). For the contrast IMI>CT we found activations in the core areas of the MNS [inferior parietal lobule (IPL) and inferior frontal cortex, the posterior part of pars opercularis], as well as in areas related to the MS [superior temporal sulcus (STS) and middle cingulate cortex]. For S>NS, we found activations in the left medial orbitofrontal cortex (mOFC), right superior frontal cortex and middle cingulate cortex. The interaction of stimulus condition (S vs NS) and task (IMI vs CT) revealed activation in the right IPL. For the interaction between observation vs execution (O vs E), task (IMI vs CT) and stimulus condition (S vs NS) we found activation in the right mOFC. Our data suggest that imitation is differentially processed in the MNS as well as in the MS. The activation in IPL is enhanced during the processing of social gestures most likely due to their communicative intention. The activation of IPL together with medial frontal areas may contribute to mentalizing processes. The interaction in the mOFC suggests an involvement of self-referential processes in the processing of social gesture.

studies.title: Frontal Control Over Automatic Emotional Action Tendencies Predicts Acute Stress Responsivity.
studies.abstract: The ability to control social-emotional actions is relevant for everyday social interaction and may be indicative of responsiveness to actual social stress situations. This is particularly relevant for predicting stress responsiveness of the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis, known to be dysregulated in various stress-related affective disorders. Here we tested, in a large sample, whether reduced frontal control over social approach-avoidance actions can indeed signal increased hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis reactivity to subsequent social stress exposure.

studies.title: Concrete versus abstract forms of social concept: an fMRI comparison of knowledge about people versus social terms.
studies.abstract: The anterior temporal lobes (ATLs) play a key role in conceptual knowledge representation. The hub-and-spoke theory suggests that the contribution of the ATLs to semantic representation is (a) transmodal, i.e. integrating information from multiple sensorimotor and verbal modalities, and (b) pan-categorical, representing concepts from all categories. Another literature, however, suggests that this region's responses are modality- and category-selective; prominent examples include category selectivity for socially relevant concepts and face recognition. The predictions of each approach have never been directly compared. We used data from three studies to compare category-selective responses within the ATLs. Study 1 compared ATL responses to famous people versus another conceptual category (landmarks) from visual versus auditory inputs. Study 2 compared ATL responses to famous people from pictorial and written word inputs. Study 3 compared ATL responses to a different kind of socially relevant stimuli, namely abstract non-person-related words, in order to ascertain whether ATL subregions are engaged for social concepts more generally or only for person-related knowledge. Excluded because the study tests adolescents with autism (and typically developing adolescents) rather than healthy adults. Inclusion met: I1 (fMRI during a social joint-attention task). Inclusion not met: I2 (no healthy participant group aged 18–65 reported). Exclusion criteria: none met (E1 not applicable).

fMRI study in healthy adult participants (n=22) investigating processing of affective/social touch and associated social perception/cognition brain regions (mPFC, STS, insula, amygdala), meeting social-related task requirement and healthy adult sample.

Exclusion E1 met: this paper is a review (not original empirical fMRI). Inclusion criteria met: none. Inclusion criteria not met/not demonstrated: I1 (no original fMRI scan while participants performed a social task reported), I2 (no report of an eligible healthy adult participant group). Exclude with high confidence based on abstract alone.

This is an fMRI study of Theory of Mind (social cognition) involving 19 healthy subjects scanned during a social-related task (REMICS). It meets I1 (social fMRI task) and I2 (healthy participant group). Age range not specified but abstract indicates healthy adults; include for full-text verification.

Study used fMRI in healthy adult participants (18 male non-musicians) and the task elicited Theory-of-Mind/social-cognition activations (PCC/PC, arMFC, TPJ), indicating measurement of social-related processing. Therefore inclusion criteria I1 and I2 are met; no exclusion criteria apply.

E1: This article is a voxel-based meta-analysis and thus meets the exclusion criterion for meta-analyses. Abstract reports fMRI studies of mother–infant interaction and oxytocin modulation (meets I1: social-related fMRI task). The abstract does not clearly state that included participants were healthy adults aged 18–65 (I2 not demonstrated).

No exclusion criteria met. Inclusion criteria met: none. Inclusion criteria not met: I1 — study used resting-state fMRI, not a task-based social processing fMRI; I2 — participants are children/adolescents with ASD and age-matched controls (not healthy adults aged 18–65).

Exclusion IDs met: none. Inclusion IDs met: none. Inclusion IDs not met/not demonstrated: I1 - abstract does not report an fMRI social-related task; it examines cognitive deficits and MCCB in schizophrenia, not social processing. I2 - abstract does not clearly report inclusion of a healthy adult (18–65) group; participants appear to be schizophrenia patients. Not a review (E1 not applicable). Therefore excluded based on failure to meet I1 and I2.

fMRI study of social behavior (Cyberball and modified Dictator Game) addressing social exclusion/punishment/forgiveness — meets social-related task criterion. Abstract does not report participant ages or explicitly state health status, so include for full-text review to confirm age 18–65 and health.

(a) exclusion IDs met: none; (b) inclusion IDs met: none; (c) inclusion IDs not met or not demonstrated: I2 not met — sample described as youth/pediatric (not healthy adults 18–65); I1 not demonstrated — abstract does not report an fMRI scan during a social-related task.

Abstract reports functional MRI during tasks involving social-cognition-related processes (mentalizing/trait inference), meeting I1. Participant health/age not specified in abstract, so I2 cannot be confirmed—include for full-text review to verify.

The study reports fMRI of socioemotional processing in schizophrenia patients (meets I1) but does not include any healthy adult participant group (I2 not met). No exclusion criteria (e.g., review) are met. Exclude because the review requires at least one healthy adult group.

The study used EEG to measure mu rhythm, not functional MRI; therefore it does not meet inclusion criterion I1 (requires fMRI). The abstract does describe healthy adult participants, but modality mismatch is decisive. No exclusion criteria (E1) apply.

Abstract addresses social cognition and neural activity in patients and unaffected siblings but does not explicitly state that fMRI was conducted or confirm a healthy adult control group aged 18–65. Because the abstract is insufficient to determine whether I1 and I2 are met but the study is likely relevant, include for full-text review.

Abstract reports an fMRI empathy task (social processing) and includes a healthy control group. However, ages of participants (required 18–65) are not reported in the abstract, so inclusion criterion I2 cannot be confirmed from the abstract alone. No exclusion criteria are met. Include for full-text review to verify age and other details.

Abstract reports fMRI experiments of biological motion perception—a social perception task—conducted in schizophrenia and healthy individuals. This satisfies I1 (fMRI during social-related task) and I2 (includes healthy adult group). No exclusion criteria apply.

The study used fMRI while participants performed a prosocial learning task (social processing) and examines empathy and neural mechanisms of learning for others. The sample is described as human participants (typical healthy adult sample implied). Thus it meets I1 (social fMRI task) and I2 (healthy human participants).

fMRI study examining processing of social versus nonsocial gestures (a social-related task). Abstract reports correlations with personality traits and does not indicate clinical populations; implies healthy adult participants. Study is empirical (not a review). Meets I1 and I2.

The study used resting-state fMRI (rsfMRI) before/after rTMS rather than an fMRI task assessing social-related processing, so it does not meet inclusion criterion I1. Healthy adult participants are included (I2).

Abstract reports neural correlates of mentalizing (a social-cognitive process) and brain structure differences linked to OXTR polymorphism, implying fMRI investigation of social-related processing in adults. No indication the paper is a review. Therefore it appears to meet criteria I1 (social-related fMRI task) and I2 (healthy adult participants).

Exclusion IDs met: none. Inclusion IDs met: none. Inclusion IDs not met or not demonstrated: I1 (study used resting-state fMRI, not a task-based social processing paradigm) and I2 (healthy control group mentioned but participant ages 18–65 not specified; presence of an eligible healthy adult group is not demonstrated). Therefore exclude based on failure to meet required inclusion criteria.

This is an fMRI study of participants observing social interactions with gaze manipulation, addressing social cognition—meets I1. The abstract does not specify participant ages or health status, so I2 cannot be confirmed; include for full-text review.

The fMRI study required participants to trace emotional content of vocalizations and music, a task involving perception/understanding of others (social cognition). No clinical groups or review status are reported; participants are presumably healthy adults. Meets I1 and I2.

E1 met: this is a review article (Progress in Brain Research chapter) rather than primary empirical fMRI research. Inclusion criteria met: none. Inclusion criteria not met/not demonstrated: I1 (no original fMRI scan during a social task reported), I2 (no healthy adult participants; the paper focuses on infants/early development).

Study used fMRI during a social interaction task (iterated Prisoner’s Dilemma) in healthy subjects randomized to intranasal oxytocin or placebo — meets the review objective. Ages not specified in the abstract, so include for full-text review to confirm age range (18–65).

Abstract reports dyadic fMRI during eye contact and derives neural bases for reciprocal social interaction, indicating a social-related task using fMRI (meets I1). The abstract does not specify participant ages or health status, so I2 cannot be confirmed from the abstract; include for full-text review to verify I2.

fMRI was used while participants engaged in live, contingent social interactions and joint attention tasks (social cognitive processing). The abstract implies a typical healthy participant sample with no clinical groups reported. Thus inclusion criteria I1 and I2 are met.

This is an fMRI study of facial emotion recognition (social communication/perception) in 29 healthy subjects. It reports neural responses during explicit and implicit emotion processing, meeting I1 (social-related fMRI task) and I2 (healthy adult participants). No exclusion criteria apply.

The study used an fMRI social cognition task (comic strip task probing Theory of Mind and empathy), satisfying I1. The abstract does not specify participant health status or ages 18–65, so I2 is not demonstrated from the abstract. No exclusion criteria met. Because participant health/age are unclear, include for full-text review to confirm eligibility.

fMRI was used while participants viewed social vs non-social pictures (meets I1). The study includes a healthy control group, though ages 18–65 are not specified in the abstract (I2 not fully confirmed). No exclusion criteria met. Include for full-text review to confirm participant ages and extract data.

Exclusion IDs met: none. Inclusion IDs met: I1 (fMRI acquired during an affective mentalizing/social cognition task). Inclusion IDs not met: I2 (no group of healthy adults aged 18–65 — comparison group are nonpsychotic criminal offenders, not healthy controls). Therefore excluded on basis of lacking healthy adult participants.

fMRI task involved processing facial expressions of emotion—a social-related task satisfying I1. The abstract reports healthy control participants, but does not state participant ages, so I2 (age 18–65) cannot be confirmed from abstract alone. No exclusion criteria met. Full-text review needed to confirm ages and sample details.

fMRI study addresses social-related processing (gaze direction), satisfying I1. A typically developing comparison group is present, but the abstract does not specify ages 18–65 so I2 is not confirmed. No exclusion criteria met. Include for full-text review to confirm healthy participants’ ages and other details.

Abstract describes methodological analysis of brain network community structure during rest and task states, with no mention of social-related tasks or social processing. Inclusion criterion I1 (social-related fMRI task) is not met.

Sample consists of adolescents rather than adults (not within 18–65), and the fMRI task (Monetary Incentive Delay) is a monetary reward task rather than an explicitly social-related task. Therefore the study does not meet inclusion criteria I1 or I2 based on the abstract.

Abstract indicates investigation of social-cognitive/neurobiological alterations in psychopathy but does not specify that an fMRI task was used (I1 unclear) nor whether healthy adult participants were included (I2 unclear). Not a review/meta-analysis (E1 not met). Insufficient information to confirm inclusion criteria from abstract alone — include for full-text review.

Participants are young children (4 and 6 years old); no adult participants aged 18–65 are included. Therefore the study does not meet inclusion criterion I2 requiring at least one healthy adult group. Abstract provides no evidence of an adult sample, so exclude.

fMRI study where participants judged and conceptualized actions; task taps perception/understanding of others and mental-state reasoning, fitting social-related processing (I1). Abstract does not specify participant ages or explicitly state healthy adult sample, so I2 cannot be confirmed from the abstract; include for full-text review to verify I2.

fMRI was conducted during retrieval in the scanner for collaboratively vs individually learned labels, a social communication/understanding of others task; participants described as healthy human adults. Meets I1 and I2.

Whole-brain fMRI was conducted while participants viewed faces of other group members, examining social cognition and valuation related to others' popularity (social perception/understanding of others). No clinical populations are mentioned, implying healthy adult participants. Thus it meets I1 and I2.

Abstract reports an fMRI study of multimodal perception of nonverbal emotional social signals (meets I1). The abstract does not specify participant health status or ages (I2 unclear). No exclusion criteria met. Insufficient information on participant age/health in abstract, so include for full-text review to confirm I2.

Abstract reports an fMRI threat-reactivity task using socially threatening images (meets I1: social-related task) and includes a healthy control group of age-matched women with no cancer history (meets I2). Not a review/meta-analysis (E1 not met).

Abstract reports an fMRI study of face emotion processing (a social-related task) in a community sample (likely healthy). Age range not specified, and health status/ages cannot be fully confirmed from the abstract, so include for full-text review to verify I2.

Participants were children/adolescents (not adults aged 18–65), so inclusion criterion I2 is not met. The study used fMRI with a social-related task (I1 met). No exclusion criteria are met (not a review).

No exclusion criteria met. Inclusion met: I1 (fMRI task assessing social cognition/ToM). Inclusion NOT met: I2 — sample are children aged 9–13, not healthy adults age 18–65 required for the review. Abstract clearly reports participant ages, so exclude based on age criterion.

Abstract reports an fMRI study in healthy young adults performing an incentive delay task including social reward processing (anticipation and feedback). This satisfies inclusion of an fMRI social-related task and healthy participants aged within 18–65. Not a review/meta-analysis.

No exclusion criteria met (E1 not applicable). Inclusion I1 (fMRI during a social-related task) is not demonstrated in the abstract (connectivity analysis described but task not specified). Inclusion I2 (healthy adults age 18–65) is not met — participants are adolescents. Therefore exclude.

Abstract reports fMRI responses to moral sentiments (guilt) and study of proneness to social/moral emotions in healthy individuals, indicating an fMRI social-related task (I1). Age range not specified, so inclusion on I2 cannot be confirmed from abstract; include for full-text review to verify participant ages. No exclusion criteria met.

fMRI was used while participants performed social-related tasks (IAT about adultery and dating ratings), targeting affiliation/attachment and social decision-making. Participants are healthy adult males in romantic relationships. Thus meets I1 and I2 based on the abstract.

Abstract provides insufficient information to confirm key inclusion criteria: it does not state that participants underwent an fMRI scan during a social-related task (I1) nor that a healthy adult group (age 18–65) was included (I2). No exclusion criteria are met. Include for full-text review to determine whether I1 and/or I2 are satisfied.

The study used fMRI to investigate social understanding (social-related task) and includes a matched healthy adult control group, satisfying I1 and I2. It is an original research article, not a review. Abstract provides sufficient information to include for full-text review.

fMRI study examining neural representations of self (social cognition) during self-judgment tasks across cultures; involves healthy adult participants. Meets criteria for social-related fMRI task and includes healthy adult group.

fMRI study where 20 typical (healthy) participants performed a social attribution task (self/other/situation), directly addressing social cognition. Meets I1 (task during fMRI) and I2 (healthy adults). Not a review or meta-analysis.

No task-based social processing — study used resting-state fMRI (I1 not met). Healthy controls are included but adult age range (18–65) is not reported in abstract (I2 not demonstrated). Not a review/meta-analysis (E1 not met). Excluding based on failure to meet inclusion criteria I1 (and I2 not demonstrated).

Abstract reports fMRI during auditory (voice) stimulation addressing voice processing and social cognition, meeting I1. Participant health/age not specified in abstract, so I2 cannot be confirmed from abstract alone; include for full-text review to verify participant characteristics.

No social task was used: resting-state fMRI only, so I1 is not met. The abstract reports healthy controls but does not report ages (I2 not demonstrated). No exclusion criteria met (E1 not applicable). Therefore exclude.

Abstract reports an fMRI neuroimaging study investigating interpersonal synchrony and social affiliation with behavioral and neuroimaging results implicating social-cognition areas. Participants (N=100) served as referents and no clinical populations are mentioned, satisfying I1 (fMRI during social-related task) and I2 (healthy adult participants implied). Age range not specified but no disorders reported—include for full-text confirmation if needed.

Study used task-based fMRI to examine neural responses to social inclusion/exclusion (social processing) in human participants; meets age/group criterion implied (healthy adult participants). Not a review. Abstract provides sufficient detail to include for full-text screening.

Abstract reports an fMRI study using a social exclusion/performance task (meets I1). The sample health status and ages are not specified in the abstract, so inclusion regarding healthy adults (I2) cannot be confirmed from abstract alone; full-text review is warranted.

Abstract reports an fMRI study of Theory of Mind (a social cognition task) and includes healthy comparison subjects; age range of healthy participants (18–65) is not specified in the abstract, so full-text review is needed to confirm I2.

Abstract examines neural bases of emotional sentence attribution (a social-related task) but does not explicitly state that fMRI was used or that healthy adult controls (age 18–65) were included. Insufficient information — include for full-text review.

fMRI study used a false-belief task probing understanding of others' mental states, satisfying I1 (social-related task). The abstract does not explicitly state participants were healthy adults aged 18–65, so I2 is not demonstrated from the abstract. No exclusion criteria apply. Include for full-text review to confirm participant health and ages.

E1 met: this paper is an activation likelihood estimation meta-analysis. Inclusion criteria met: none clearly met from the abstract. Inclusion criteria not demonstrated: I1 (abstract does not clearly state tasks were social-related social-processing rather than general speech perception), I2 (abstract does not specify that healthy participants were adults age 18–65).

Abstract reports an event-related fMRI study of moral reasoning (a social-related task) and includes a healthy control group matched for age, gender, and education. Age range 18–65 is not explicitly stated in the abstract, so full text is needed to confirm I2. Include for full-text review to verify participant ages and other details.

E1 met: this study is a meta-analysis/systematic review rather than an original fMRI experiment. Inclusion criteria met: none. Inclusion criteria not met/not demonstrated: I1 (no original fMRI scan while participants performed a social task reported), I2 (no explicit report of a group of healthy adults aged 18–65 in the abstract).
Participants are children with ASD and age-matched typically developing children (not adults). No group of healthy adults (age 18–65) is included, so study fails inclusion criterion I2.

Event-related fMRI study of social gaze/intent processing (meets I1). Includes a group of typically developing (healthy) subjects (n=9), meeting I2. Not a review or meta-analysis (E1 not met). Abstract provides sufficient information to include for full-text review.

The study used fMRI while participants viewed faces of political candidates (a social perception/understanding of others task) and involved healthy adult participants (registered Democrats and Republicans). Thus it meets I1 and I2. No exclusion criteria (e.g., not a review) apply. Include for full-text review.

fMRI was used to measure brain activity during biological motion processing (a social perception task), and the study included a group of healthy matched controls. Not a review/meta-analysis and meets social-related task criterion.

Excluded because abstract reports fMRI social-cognition in patients with schizophrenia but does not report any healthy adult control group. Inclusion met: I1 (fMRI during a social-related task). Inclusion not met: I2 (at least one healthy participants group age 18–65) not demonstrated. Exclusion criteria met: none (E1 not applicable).

Abstract reports task-based fMRI of personality judgments about self and familiar other (meets I1). However participants are adult incarcerated offenders with no healthy control group described, so I2 is not met. No exclusion criteria apply (E1 not met). Exclude based on lack of healthy participants in abstract.

Abstract reports fMRI during a charitable donation task (social/altruistic decision-making), meeting I1. The abstract does not specify participants' health status or ages 18–65 (I2 not demonstrated). Not a review (no exclusions). Include for full-text review to confirm I2.

fMRI was used while participants performed a trustworthiness ratings task (a social cognition task), meeting I1. Abstract implies human participants but does not specify ages or health status, so full text is needed to confirm I2.

Abstract reports an fMRI task probing recall of relationship episodes (self/others) in 35 healthy individuals—fits social-related processing and fMRI (I1). Age range (18–65) is not reported in the abstract, so inclusion should be confirmed at full-text stage (I2 not verifiable from abstract). Include for full-text review to verify participant ages and other details.

Functional MRI was used while healthy volunteers performed social tasks (empathy and forgivability judgments), directly addressing social-related processing. Although participant ages are not specified, the sample of 'ten volunteers' is consistent with adult healthy participants; include for full-text review to confirm ages and details.

This fMRI study used a faces vs objects viewing paradigm—face perception is a social-related process (Perception/Understanding of Others), meeting I1. The sample spans from childhood through adulthood and reports adult participants (presumably healthy), satisfying I2. No exclusion criteria apply. Abstract provides sufficient information to include for full-text review.

Abstract does not report an fMRI social-related task (I1 not demonstrated) nor specify inclusion of healthy adults aged 18–65 (I2 not demonstrated); it is not a systematic review (E1 not met). Insufficient information to determine eligibility from abstract alone — include for full-text review.

The study uses fMRI and investigates social cognition (representing what another person sees/joint attention), meeting I1. The abstract does not specify participant health status or ages (18–65), so I2 cannot be confirmed from the abstract; therefore include for full-text review to verify eligibility.

Included for full-text review: fMRI was used while participants anticipated others’ actions (perception/understanding of others), meeting I1. The abstract does not report participant ages or explicitly confirm health status, so I2 cannot be confirmed from abstract alone; exclusion E1 not met.

fMRI was used while participants attended to the social meaning of symbolic artifacts, engaging social cognition regions (mPFC, TPJ), satisfying I1. The abstract does not explicitly report participant ages or explicitly state ‘healthy adults,’ so I2 is unclear; include for full-text review to confirm demographics.

fMRI study examining emotion and social cognition during legal decision-making (social cognition/perception of others) — meets I1. Abstract does not report participant ages or explicit statement of healthy adults, so I2 is unclear; include for full-text review to confirm. No exclusion criteria met.

Abstract reports an fMRI study where healthy adult women viewed social interaction animations (social perception task), satisfying social-related task requirement. Participants were healthy adults (women not using hormonal contraception), meeting the healthy sample criterion. No exclusion criteria apply.

This is an fMRI study of social processing (learning others' trustworthiness) involving healthy younger and older participants. It meets I1 (social-related task during fMRI) and appears to meet I2 (includes a healthy younger adult group likely within 18–65). No exclusion criteria apply.

Abstract reports task-based fMRI probing self- and other-related social cognition and reports a healthy control group; meets social-related fMRI and healthy-participant inclusion criteria. No exclusion criteria met. Include for full-text to confirm participant ages and specific task details.

The study uses fMRI during processing of emotional faces, a social perception task (meets I1). The abstract does not specify participant health status or ages (I2 not demonstrated). Not a review (E1 not met). Include for full-text review to confirm participant demographics and health status.

Study II reports functional MRI during a social-interaction/gaze paradigm (meets I1) and includes a healthy control group (n=16), meeting I2. No exclusion criteria apply. Although exact participant ages are not listed in the abstract, the presence of adult healthy controls supports inclusion for full-text review.

Abstract reports task-related fMRI during a social perception experiment (meets I1) and includes a healthy control group of adults (n=21) (meets I2). It is original research, not a review. Therefore it should be included for full-text review to confirm details.

fMRI study using MVPA of social cognition to identify neural dimensions of mental state representation — meets I1. Abstract does not report participant ages or explicitly state healthy adult sample, so full-text needed to confirm I2.

fMRI study investigating irony comprehension (a social-communication/social-cognition task) with event-related design; includes a healthy adult control group (15 female controls). No exclusion criteria met.

Abstract reports decoding performance on social cognition tasks using task fMRI from the HCP dataset; this indicates fMRI during social-related tasks. Participant health/age not explicitly stated in abstract, so full-text review is needed to confirm healthy adults. Include for full-text review.

No healthy participant group reported: study includes 25 unmedicated chronic depression patients. Inclusion met: I1 (fMRI during an affective theory-of-mind social task). Inclusion not met: I2 (no healthy adults 18–65 group). No exclusion criteria (E1) apply.

fMRI was performed during an interactive Domino task probing mentalizing/social processing (meets I1). The study includes a healthy control group of adults aged 18–34 (meets I2). Not a review/meta-analysis (E1 not met). Abstract provides sufficient information to include for full-text review.

Simultaneous fMRI was used while participants engaged in live verbal interaction (social communication), fulfilling social-related task requirement. Participants were pairs of adult female friends (healthy adults), satisfying the healthy adult group criterion. Not a review or meta-analysis.

Study used fMRI during a social-related 'social reflection' task and reports 22 healthy subjects, meeting I1. Participant ages (18–65) are not specified in the abstract, so I2 is uncertain; include for full-text review to confirm. No exclusion criteria met.

Excluded because the study used resting-state fMRI rather than a social-related task (I1 not met). Healthy volunteers are included but ages 18–65 are not reported, so I2 is not demonstrated. No exclusion criteria (E1) apply.

fMRI measured responses to faces (natural vs bluish) which is social communication/perception (facial cues), satisfying I1. Abstract reports 25 subjects but does not state ages or health status, so I2 is unclear; include for full-text review.

Study used fMRI during a social-interaction task (ultimatum game) to predict decisions in volunteers, meeting social-processing task requirement. Participants are described as volunteers (healthy adults), satisfying inclusion of healthy adult group. No exclusion criteria apply.

Event-related fMRI recorded while human subjects performed social judgments (trustworthiness of faces), clearly a social processing task. Participants are described as subjects (healthy adults implied) within typical adult age range. This meets inclusion criteria I1 and I2.

Abstract reports an fMRI study where mothers’ brain responses to emotional expressions of their own children were compared—this is a social-related task (perception/attachment). Participants are adult mothers (healthy adult group). No exclusion criteria apply. Full text recommended to confirm participant ages and health status.

Abstract reports an fMRI experiment where participants performed mentalising/theory-of-mind tasks (social cognition), satisfying I1. Abstract reports an fMRI study of social interaction (self- and other-initiated joint attention) in 24 healthy adult participants (ages within 18–65), meeting the review scope. No exclusion criteria are met. Recommend inclusion for full-text review.

fMRI study of pragmatic/social communication (integration of speaker characteristics with message content) in adults; includes a matched healthy control group of adults. Not a review. Meets inclusion criteria I1 and I2; no exclusion criteria met.

EXCLUDED: Abstract reports fMRI of social processing (I1 satisfied) but participants are described as 'youth' (ASD and age-matched typically-developing controls), not adults 18–65. Therefore I2 (healthy adult group 18–65) is not met. No exclusion criteria apply.

Excluded because the study used resting-state fMRI rather than a social-related task, so inclusion criterion I1 is not met. Inclusion criterion I2 is met (healthy adult volunteers). No exclusion criteria met (E1 not applicable).

fMRI was conducted during an ecologically valid social interaction task (Taylor Aggression Paradigm with angry/neutral facial expressions), and the sample comprised healthy adult participants (41 tested, 32 analyzed). Study uses fMRI social-evaluation task (I1 met) but participants are adolescents, not adults aged 18–65; thus inclusion criterion I2 (healthy adults 18–65) is not met. No exclusion criteria met.

Abstract reports neural-level analyses and dynamic causal modeling of empathy and mentalizing in naturalistic social tasks, implying functional neuroimaging. Excluded: No healthy adult participants (I2 not met) — participants are children (ASD and typically developing). Inclusion met: I1 (fMRI during a social/pragmatic language task). Exclusion met: none (E1 not met).

fMRI was conducted during a third-party punishment task probing attribution of intentions and moral responsibility—social cognition. Participants appear to be healthy adults. Thus it meets both I1 and I2.

Abstract reports behavioral and fMRI findings using a social attribution (mentalizing) task (meets I1) in a sample of 22 typically developing adults (meets I2). No exclusion criteria are met. Participants are adolescents (mean age 17) and no adult (18–65) group is reported, so the study fails inclusion criterion I2 (age). It does use fMRI social stimuli (I1), but age criterion not met based on abstract.

Study reports two fMRI experiments in healthy young adults performing a social attribution task (perception of human-like interactions). This meets I1 (fMRI during a social-related task) and I2 (healthy adult participants). Not a review or meta-analysis; no exclusion criteria met.

The study used fMRI during a face discrimination task (social perception—meets I1) and includes an age- and gender-matched healthy adult control group (meets I2). Ages are not numerically reported but are described as healthy adults. No exclusion criteria are met.

fMRI was used during an Implicit Association Test assessing political attitudes (social processing of others), satisfying I1. No exclusion criteria met. Inclusion criteria not satisfied: I1 not met — abstract reports fMRI connectivity and behavioral assessments but does not describe a social-related task; I2 not met — sample are children and adolescents, not healthy adults aged 18–65. Therefore exclude.

fMRI was used while participants observed dynamic and static facial expressions (a social perception task), satisfying I1. No social-related task is described; the study examines memory retrieval and white-matter/functional connectivity (I1 not met). The study used fMRI during self-reference and reference-to-others tasks, which are social-cognitive processes (Perception/Understanding of Self and Others), satisfying I1. fMRI study of self-referential processing (social-related task), meeting I1. Healthy control group is reported, but participant ages (18–65) are not specified in the abstract, so I2 cannot be confirmed from abstract alone; full-text review needed. No exclusion criteria met.

fMRI was conducted during social-related tasks (theory of mind), satisfying I1. Randomized, placebo-controlled fMRI study using the Prisoner’s Dilemma (a social interaction task) in human male and female adults, meeting I1 and I2. Not a review (E1 not met). Abstract provides sufficient information to include for full-text review.

fMRI study of social evaluation using videos in a sample of 37 healthy participants; directly investigates neural processing of social-related stimuli (social evaluation), meeting the review objective. Abstract reports an fMRI study of visual perspective selection, a social-cognition task (perspective taking). Although participant health/ages are not explicitly stated, this is a typical healthy adult cognitive neuroscience sample; include for full-text verification of demographics.

fMRI study presenting infant cries and faces (social/attachment and perception of others), satisfying I1. Participants are healthy nulliparous women with no disorders reported, satisfying I2. No exclusion criteria (E1) apply. Include for full-text review.

fulltext_screening_results.reason: This is an fMRI study of social cognition (impression formation/updating of others) using a task with faces and behaviors. Sample: 24 healthy adults, ages 18–45, meeting the adult healthy sample criterion. The paper reports group-level, whole-brain task-evoked analyses (interaction and L2>F3 contrasts) with voxelwise thresholds, cluster correction, figures and tables of results. Whole-brain results are clearly described for the healthy/control group. The full text includes Introduction, Methods, Results, and Discussion; supplemental materials are referenced but not required. Therefore it meets I3, I4, I5 and I6, and no exclusion criteria apply.

This is a task-based fMRI study of social perception (visual processing of dyadic interactions), using healthy adult participants (N=21, ages 18–35). The authors performed whole-brain preprocessing and GLM estimation to generate run-wise whole-brain beta maps and report group-level statistical analyses (one-sample t-tests) and whole-brain searchlight analyses. Results include group-level voxelwise classification/searchlight findings and discussion of whole-brain effects. Therefore the study meets inclusion criteria for: I3 (fMRI during social-related task), I4 (healthy adult sample 18–65), I5 (reports group-level whole-brain voxelwise task analyses/maps), and I6 (whole-brain results clearly described). No exclusion criteria (e.g., ROI-only or resting-state-only) apply.

This is an empirical fMRI study that directly examines understanding of others' regret (a social-related ‘perception and understanding of others’ task) using task-based BOLD fMRI. Participants are healthy adults (two samples of 24 each; ages reported within 18–65). The paper reports group-level, whole-brain voxelwise task contrasts (e.g., IP minus IF and OP minus OF), parametric and conjunction analyses, and reports activation foci/coordinates and whole-brain statistical maps described in the text and figures. Thus it meets inclusion criteria I3, I4, I5 and I6. No exclusion criteria (ROI-only, connectivity-only, between-group-only, out-of-range ages, or non-empirical) are met. Full text appears complete (includes Introduction, Methods, Results, Discussion, and acquisition/analysis details).

Exclusion E4: The study includes fMRI social tasks and a healthy control group aged 50–60 (I3 and I4 are satisfied). However, the paper does not report an unmasked, whole-brain task activation map clearly identified as coming from the healthy/control group. Reported whole-brain maps are for the combined sample (whole group) and ROI/small-volume corrected analyses and between-group contrasts (Cocaine > Control). Therefore it fails inclusion criterion I5 (no healthy-group whole-brain task effect reported) and meets exclusion criterion E4. Full text appears complete.

This is an empirical fMRI study using an ecological social-related task (listening to film excerpts and inferring characters’ mental states), including a healthy adult group (HC-S1, n=28; ages 18–65). The manuscript reports group-level, whole-brain voxelwise results for the healthy control group (INT>HIN contrast; one-sample t-test, p<0.05 FWE) with tables and figures of activation peaks and maps, satisfying whole-brain reporting requirements. Results for the healthy group are clearly separable from the patient group. Full article text (introduction, methods, results, discussion, references) is provided. No exclusion criteria (ROI-only, connectivity/resting-state-only, between-group-only maps, out-of-range ages, or non-empirical paper) are met. Therefore the study meets all inclusion criteria I3, I4, I5, and I6 and should be included in the review.
